summary: Describes the Calendar Access Protocol, which lets a calendar user use a user agent to access an iCalendar-based calendar store. Written at a time when three vendors were implementing it and changes were known to be needed, it preserves years of work to gain implementation experience. It defines an Experimental Protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: Your calendar app talks to the calendar server using this language. It is an experiment, kept so people could learn what works.

questions: how do calendar apps access servers
subtitle: A protocol for calendar applications to store and retrieve calendar information on remote servers.

tldr.problem: Calendar applications need a standard way to access and manipulate calendar data stored on remote servers, including querying, creating, and modifying events, todos, and other calendar components.
tldr.mechanism: CAP defines a BEEP-based protocol that sends iCalendar objects between a calendar client (CUA) and a calendar server (CS), with commands to create, modify, delete, and search calendar components, along with access control through Calendar Access Rights (VCAR).
tldr.outcome: Three vendors were implementing CAP at publication, but the specification remains Experimental and never became widely adopted. The protocol preserved years of work on calendar features that could be reused in other standards.

today: RFC 4324 defines an Experimental protocol that was never adopted as an Internet Standard. While three vendors were implementing CAP at the time of publication, the protocol did not achieve widespread deployment. CalDAV, published later as RFC 4791, became the dominant protocol for calendar access on the internet. However, many concepts and properties from CAP have influenced subsequent calendar and scheduling protocols.

sections.title: Calendar Access Over Networks
sections.content:
The Calendar Access Protocol (CAP) enables a calendar application—called a Calendar User Agent (CUA)—to connect to a calendar server, called a Calendar Store (CS), and manage calendar information. A CUA can query, create, modify, delete, and search for calendar events, todos, journal entries, and other components stored on a remote CS.

CAP builds on the iCalendar format (RFC 2445), which standardizes how calendar objects are represented. It also incorporates concepts from iTIP (RFC 2446), the Internet calendaring scheduling protocol. At the time CAP was written, three vendors were actively implementing it, though it has remained in Experimental status with known limitations.
sections.plainLanguage: CAP is like an instruction set that tells your calendar app how to ask a calendar server to save, find, or change your appointments.

sections.title: Architecture and Transport
sections.content:
CAP defines both an application protocol and a system model. The transport layer uses BEEP (Block Extensible Exchange Protocol), which runs over TCP and handles authentication, encryption, and session management. The default port for calendar servers is 1026.

Communication flows between the CUA and CS as MIME-encapsulated messages. A CUA sends a request in iCalendar format, and the CS responds with a reply in the same format. The protocol supports optional latency parameters and timeouts—if a command takes too long, the server can send a TIMEOUT command, and the client can choose to CONTINUE the operation or ABORT it.
sections.plainLanguage: The calendar app connects to the server using BEEP, which is like a secure telephone line. The app and server send messages back and forth formatted as calendar objects.

sections.title: Calendar Objects and Structure
sections.content:
CAP introduces several new iCalendar components to organize calendar information. The VCALSTORE is the root object representing an entire calendar server and contains multiple VAGENDA components, each representing a single calendar. A VAGENDA holds VEVENT objects (events), VTODO objects (todos), VJOURNAL objects (journal entries), and VTIMEZONE objects (timezone definitions).

Two additional components support advanced features. A VQUERY component allows clients to search for calendar objects using a query language (CAL-QUERY), with SELECT and WHERE clauses similar to SQL. A VCAR component (Calendar Access Rights) specifies who can perform which operations on which calendar objects.

Objects in the calendar store have conceptual states: BOOKED (a confirmed calendar entry), UNPROCESSED (a scheduling message awaiting decision), or DELETED (marked for deletion but retained for synchronization purposes).
sections.plainLanguage: A calendar server contains calendars, which contain events and todos. You can search for specific events using queries. The server also tracks who is allowed to see or change each event.

sections.title: Commands and Operations
sections.content:
CAP supports several core commands for manipulating calendar data. The CREATE command stores one or more new iCalendar objects in the calendar store in either BOOKED or UNPROCESSED state. The DELETE command removes objects or marks them as deleted. The MODIFY command updates existing objects. The MOVE command relocates objects between containers.

The SEARCH command queries the calendar store using CAL-QUERY, a search language that allows clients to specify which properties to retrieve and which objects to match. For example, a client can search for all VEVENT objects with a given UID, or all events in a date range, with optional expansion of recurring instances into multiple objects.

Other commands include GENERATE-UID (to obtain unique identifiers from the server), IDENTIFY (to establish the caller's identity within the session), GET-CAPABILITY (to learn what the server supports), and SET-LOCALE (to switch languages and character sets).
sections.plainLanguage: The app can tell the server to create, change, or delete events; search for specific events; and ask the server what features it supports.

sections.title: Access Control and Permissions
sections.content:
CAP implements fine-grained access control through Calendar Access Rights (VCAR components). A VCAR contains one or more VRIGHT components, each defining a set of permissions granted or denied to specific users or groups.

A VRIGHT specifies which operations (SEARCH, CREATE, DELETE, MODIFY, or MOVE) are permitted, to which objects (defined by a scope query), and for which users (identified by User Principal Names, or UPNs). For example, a VRIGHT might grant search permission on all VEVENT objects to a specific user, or grant full permissions to the calendar owner.

The server enforces these rights based on the authenticated identity of the CUA's session. Different calendars can have different access rights, and the same user can have different permissions depending on the calendar.
sections.plainLanguage: Each calendar keeps a list of rules saying which users can do what—search, add, change, or delete events. The server checks these rules when the app asks to do something.

sections.title: Experimental Status and Limitations
sections.content:
CAP is defined as an Experimental protocol and never advanced to Standard status. At the time of publication, three vendors were implementing it, but the specification explicitly noted that changes were already known to be needed. The protocol was published in Experimental status to preserve years of work on calendar properties and parameters that could benefit other iCalendar standards.

CAP did not achieve widespread deployment. Other calendar access protocols, particularly CalDAV (defined years later), became more widely adopted for accessing calendar servers. However, many of the properties, parameters, and concepts defined in CAP have influenced subsequent calendar protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: This protocol was an experiment. Three companies were trying it out, but it never became the standard way calendar apps talk to servers. However, many ideas from it helped make better calendar protocols later.
